props.title: The Rum Diary

sections.content: The Rum Diary (2011) marks Johnny Depp's second venture into Hunter S. Thompson territory after Fear and Loathing in Las Vegas (1998). Based on Thompson's early novel, it captures his pre-gonzo years as a struggling journalist in Puerto Rico. The film channels 1960s Caribbean chaos through a booze-soaked lens, with Depp playing Paul Kemp, Thompson's alter ego. While lacking the hallucinatory madness of Fear and Loathing, it shares DNA with sun-drenched journalism films like Salvador (1986) and The Year of Living Dangerously (1982) - stories of American writers discovering their voice amid tropical political upheaval.

sections.content: Director Bruce Robinson, himself known for the cult classic Withnail & I (1987), brings a similarly boozy energy to The Rum Diary's portrayal of expatriate life. The film works best as a origin story for Thompson's signature style, showing how righteous anger at corruption and capitalism's excesses would later fuel his gonzo journalism. Aaron Eckhart's sleazy real estate developer Sanderson represents the American exploitation that Thompson would spend his career raging against, while Giovanni Ribisi channels the chemical experimentation that would become legendary in Thompson's later work.

The film connects to a broader tradition of journalists-abroad narratives like The Quiet American (2002) and The Killing Fields (1984), where idealistic reporters confront harsh political realities. But The Rum Diary is ultimately more interested in capturing a specific moment - both in Thompson's evolution and in pre-tourist Puerto Rico - than in hard-hitting journalism. The romance with Amber Heard's Chenault occasionally derails the political elements, but serves to highlight Kemp/Thompson's competing desires for comfort versus truth-telling. sections.content: Beyond The Rum Diary, Thompson's influence echoes through films like Buy the Ticket, Take the Ride (2006) and Gonzo: The Life and Work of Dr. Hunter S. Thompson (2008). His larger-than-life persona and distinctive prose style created a template for counterculture journalism that influenced everything from Almost Famous (2000) to The Wolf of Wall Street (2013). The Rum Diary captures Thompson before the famous persona took hold, showing the rawer elements that would later define gonzo journalism.
